scimon.text: Consider the following context: Noble metal–based high-entropy alloys (NM-HEAs) are promising catalysts because of their diverse compositions and complex surface structures, although understanding their formation and achieving precise atomic control remain challenging. In that context, which method can be used for produce HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks, and why?

hidden_target.material_initial_state: Aqueous, homogeneously mixed precursor salts—(NH4)2PtCl6 and selected Co, Cu, Ni, Fe, Ru, Ir, and/or Pd salts with NH4Cl—were spray-dried into near-spherical, compositionally uniform precursor particles. The studied compositions ranged from quinary to octonary noble-metal/transition-metal mixtures.
hidden_target.intervention: The authors developed a spray-drying/thermal decomposition-reduction (SD-TDR) synthesis of noble-metal high-entropy-alloy three-dimensional nanoframeworks (HEA-3DNFs). Spray drying used a 180°C inlet, 250 ml/hour feed, 1.3 liter/s high-pressure gas flow, and 35 m3/hour drying-gas flow. Precursors were then heated in H2 at 3°C/min to 300°C for 30 min and cooled at 5°–10°C/min. They also varied Pt:Ru ratios from 3:1 to 1:4 and applied secondary heating at 400° or 500°C to tune fcc/hcp phase content; MOR activity, formation pathways, and phase transformation were investigated experimentally and by DFT.
hidden_target.conditions: Synthesis/reduction was performed in H2, normally at 300°C for 30 min; comparison reductions included 200°C and 450°C, and phase-tuning reheating used 400°–500°C. MOR was measured in deoxygenated aqueous 0.5 M H2SO4 plus 0.5 M CH3OH by cyclic voltammetry at 50 mV/s over −0.22 to 0.98 V versus Ag/AgCl, with chronoamperometry at 0.65 V for 2000 s. In situ STEM followed Pt1Ni1Co1Cu1Ru4 from room temperature to 500°C. DFT used Pt(111), Ir(111), Ru(011), and Pd(111) surfaces.
hidden_target.structural_mediator: The intervention generated porous, self-supported 3D nanoframeworks assembled from nanoarms, generally with homogeneous elemental distributions and single-phase solid-solution lattices. Pt- and Ir-based alloys adopted fcc structures, whereas Ru-based alloys adopted hcp structures. In PtxNiCoCuRuy alloys, the relative amounts and coexistence of Pt-based fcc and Ru-based hcp domains mediated the tunable structural response.
hidden_target.mechanism: The proposed, experimentally and computationally supported mechanism is that Pt, Ir, or Ru salts reduce first below 300°C and establish their characteristic lattice. H2 then adsorbs and dissociates on the newborn noble-metal surface, and readily desorbed, highly reactive H atoms reduce nearby Ni, Co, Cu, and Fe; these atoms enter the pre-existing noble-metal lattice to form a single-phase solid solution. Pd is ineffective because H desorption is unfavorable and has a higher barrier. For Pt–Ru alloys, the initially formed Pt-fcc phase is kinetically retained, although Ru-hcp is calculated to be more stable; secondary heating activates atoms to overcome the approximately 0.45-eV barrier and permits fcc-to-hcp transformation.
hidden_target.predicted_outcome: Relative to commercial Pt black, the porous single-phase PtNiCoCuRuIr HEA-3DNF was expected to show substantially greater methanol-oxidation mass activity and sustained current because of its larger electrochemically active surface area and multielement framework. Relative to unreheated or Pt-rich PtNiCoCuRu alloys, increasing Ru content and reheating temperature was expected to increase the Ru-hcp fraction and enable controlled fcc-to-hcp conversion.
hidden_target.baseline: The catalytic baseline was commercial Johnson Matthey Pt black, with 170 mA/mgPt MOR mass activity and an electrochemically active surface area of 17.59 m2/gPt. Mechanistic controls included NiCoCuFe without a noble metal, which was not reduced at 300°C and became phase-separated at 450°C, and PdNiCoCuFe, which also formed segregated multiphase material rather than a single-phase HEA. For phase control, the baseline was the predominantly Pt-based fcc PtNiCoCuRu material produced at 300°C without secondary heating.
hidden_target.boundary: The low-temperature single-phase formation mechanism held for systems seeded by Pt, Ir, or Ru under H2 but not for PdNiCoCuFe or noble-metal-free NiCoCuFe under the tested conditions. The reported phase tuning applies to PtxNiCoCuRuy HEA-3DNFs over Pt:Ru ratios of 3:1 to 1:4 and treatments of 300°–500°C: Ru enrichment and higher temperature increased hcp content, but Ru enrichment alone at 300°C did not necessarily yield a predominantly hcp material. Transition temperatures depended on composition (approximately 400°C for the observed Pt1Ni1Co1Cu1Ru4 region and 450°C for Pt1Ni1Co1Cu1Ru2).
hidden_target.discriminating_measurement: CV-derived MOR peak mass activity and chronoamperometry discriminated catalytic performance from Pt black. XRD, atomic-resolution HAADF/ABF-STEM with FFT, STEM-EDS, SEM, XPS, and ICP-MS tested phase purity, lattice structure, porosity, reduction, and elemental homogeneity. Temperature-resolved in situ HAADF-STEM directly tested fcc-to-hcp conversion, while DFT free-energy profiles, cohesive energies, and barriers tested the proposed hydrogen-assisted reduction and phase-transition mechanisms.
hidden_target.actual_result: Pt-, Ir-, Ru-, and PtRu-based quinary-to-octonary HEA-3DNFs were obtained under mild conditions. PtNiCoCuRuIr reached 2637 mA/mgPt MOR mass activity (1054.23 mA/mgPtIrRu), about 15 times Pt black on a Pt-mass basis and about 6 times on a PtIrRu-mass basis; its electrochemically active surface area was 104.4 m2/gPt, and its chronoamperometric current remained higher than Pt black throughout the measured interval. Pt, Ir, and Ru enabled single-phase HEA formation at 300°C, whereas Pd and noble-metal-free controls segregated. For phase control, increasing Ru content and reheating increased the hcp fraction: Pt1Ni1Co1Cu1Ru4 contained both fcc and hcp at 300°C and became predominantly hcp after 500°C reheating. In situ STEM directly observed hcp appearing near 350°C and complete local fcc-to-hcp conversion by 400°C in Pt1Ni1Co1Cu1Ru4, with the hcp phase remaining stable on further heating and cooling.
